title: Hot-Season Hydraulic Fault Pattern
body: When five excavators (plus one borrowed grader) all threw hydraulic faults in the same window last June, the workshop chased each symptom separately instead of the heat-stress root cause — EX-263 alone burned six straight zero-availability days, then kept resurfacing with a new hydraulic fault every time a fix looked like it had held.
keyPoints: Heat doesn't produce one repeating fault — it produces leaks, slow cylinders, and valve failures all from the same root cause (fluid viscosity drop, thermal stress on the circuit). A machine cycling through several different hydraulic symptoms in two weeks is one system problem, not several.
Dust-clogged cooler fins are a known summer aggravator — a fleet-wide cooler/radiator and oil-temperature check catches this before it becomes a breakdown, not after.

Don't bucket a mechanical failure with a hydraulic one just because they showed up together — EX-123's slew ring bearing failure got logged alongside hydraulic leak/cylinder symptoms, and nobody confirmed whether they were actually connected.

A symptom-by-symptom repair on a heat-stressed machine buys one clean day, then the fault comes back in a new form — EX-263 proved this twice. If a unit is on its third-plus hydraulic fault this season, it needs a full circuit strip (pump, cooler, lines), not another patch.
No comparative baseline exists yet for this pattern — start logging which units fault and which don't (EX-340, EX-253 stayed clean) so next hot season isn't guessing again.
apply: Any excavator throwing a hydraulic-temperature-high or leak fault today — treat it as a cooler/dust-ingress check first, not just a seal or hose swap, especially with hot-season conditions still in play.
